concept: Given a string containing only the characters '(', ')', '{', '}', '[' and ']', determine if the input string is valid. A string is valid if every opening bracket has a matching closing bracket in the correct order.

solutions.label: Brute Force with Repeated Replacement
solutions.summary: Repeatedly scan the string and remove adjacent matching pairs until no more can be removed. If the string becomes empty, it is balanced.

solutions.label: Stack-Based Matching
solutions.summary: Use a stack to push opening brackets and pop when a matching closing bracket appears. If the stack is empty at the end, the string is balanced.

sections.title: Understanding the Problem
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["Input: '( { [ ] } )'"] --> B{"Is every bracket matched?"}
    B -->|Yes| C["Return true"]
    D["Input: '( { [ ) } ]'"] --> E{"Is every bracket matched?"}

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here's the problem. You're given a string that contains only bracket characters: round parentheses, curly braces, and square brackets. You need to determine whether the string is valid, meaning every opening bracket has a matching closing bracket in the correct nesting order.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. So the string only contains these six characters and nothing else? And I return true if they're all properly matched and nested?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Exactly. The string will only have bracket characters. For example, open paren, open curly, open square, close square, close curly, close paren would be valid. But open paren, close curly would not.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: What about edge cases? Should an empty string return true? And what's the maximum length?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: An empty string is considered valid, so return true. The length can be up to ten thousand characters.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Understood. So I need to check that each opening bracket has a matching closing bracket of the same type, and they must be correctly nested. Let me think about approaches.

sections.title: Brute Force with Repeated Replacement
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["'( { [ ] } )'"] -->|"Find '[ ]'"| B["'( { } )'"]
    B -->|"Find '{ }'"| C["'( )'"]
    C -->|"Find '( )'"| D["'' (empty)"]
    D --> E["Empty → return true"]
    style A fill:#60a5fa,color:#000
    style B fill:#60a5fa,color:#000
    style C fill:#60a5fa,color:#000
    style D fill:#60a5fa,color:#000
    style E fill:#4ade80,color:#000

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: My first idea is a brute force approach. I can repeatedly scan the string for adjacent matching pairs like open paren close paren, open curly close curly, or open square close square, and remove them. I keep doing this until no more pairs can be removed.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Okay, walk me through an example.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Take the string open paren, open curly, open square, close square, close curly, close paren. First pass, I find the adjacent pair open square close square and remove it, leaving open paren, open curly, close curly, close paren. Next pass, I remove open curly close curly. Then I remove open paren close paren. The string is empty, so I return true.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What's the time complexity of this approach?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Each pass scans the string in O of n time, and in the worst case I remove one pair per pass, so there could be n over two passes. That gives O of n-squared overall. Space is O of n for creating new strings.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Can you do better than n-squared?

sections.title: Stack-Based Matching
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["Read '('"] -->|Push| B["Stack: ( "]
    B --> C["Read '{' "]
    C -->|Push| D["Stack: ( { "]
    D --> E["Read '[' "]
    E -->|Push| F["Stack: ( { [ "]
    F --> G["Read ']' "]
    G -->|"Pop '[', match!"| H["Stack: ( { "]
    H --> I["Read '}' "]
    I -->|"Pop '{', match!"| J["Stack: ( "]
    J --> K["Read ')' "]
    K -->|"Pop '(', match!"| L["Stack: empty"]
    L --> M["Empty → return true"]
    style A fill:#a78bfa,color:#000
    style D fill:#a78bfa,color:#000
    style F fill:#a78bfa,color:#000
    style H fill:#a78bfa,color:#000
    style J fill:#a78bfa,color:#000
    style L fill:#a78bfa,color:#000
    style M fill:#4ade80,color:#000

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Yes. I can use a stack. I iterate through the string once. When I see an opening bracket, I push it onto the stack. When I see a closing bracket, I pop from the stack and check if it matches. If the stack is empty at the end, the string is valid.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Walk me through the same example using the stack.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: For open paren, open curly, open square, close square, close curly, close paren: I push open paren, then open curly, then open square. Now I see close square. I pop open square from the stack — they match. Then close curly — I pop open curly, they match. Then close paren — I pop open paren, match again. Stack is empty, so return true.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What happens if there's a mismatch or the stack is empty when you try to pop?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: If I try to pop from an empty stack or the popped bracket doesn't match the current closing bracket, I immediately return false. I can use a hash map to store the mapping from closing brackets to their matching opening brackets for quick lookup.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: And the complexity?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Time complexity is O of n since I traverse the string once. Space complexity is O of n in the worst case, when all characters are opening brackets and they all get pushed onto the stack.

sections.diagram:
graph LR

O of n-squared time
O of n space"] --> B["Stack-Based
O of n time
O of n space"]
    style A fill:#60a5fa,color:#000

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great. Let's recap the two approaches.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The brute force repeatedly removes adjacent matching pairs, running in O of n-squared time. The stack approach processes each character once, giving us O of n time and O of n space. The stack solution is the standard way to solve bracket matching problems because the last-in first-out property naturally handles nesting.
